header.subject: MACRO
header.exam_format: Sec A: 20 MCQ (2M); Sec B: 4 short conceptual (5M, 50-80 words); Sec C: 2 case-based (10M, 100-150 words); Sec D: 2 higher-order subjective (10M, 100-150 words). No negative marking. 60 min.
header.style_profile: CLA (macro.docx) MCQs are CAUSAL-CHAIN: a scenario/shock, then the directional effect on a macro variable (e.g. 'exports rise, imports unchanged -> open-economy GDP identity -> GDP increases'). Distractors reverse the arrow, give the null effect, or name an adjacent variable. The written sections (B/C/D) demand the TRANSMISSION MECHANISM and correct TIMEFRAME (short-run vs long-run), grounded in the given case - not just the endpoint. Test causal DIRECTION explicitly.
header.extraction_note: FULLY VERBATIM: all four modules (M1-M4) of Principles of Macroeconomics were read in full from the lecture transcripts and every node is source-grounded. No outline-based or unverified nodes remain.
header.timeframe_tagging: Every node carries a 'timeframe' field per the subject registry (short-run / long-run / both / structural-accounting).

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Micro vs macro; aggregation over space & time
nodes.teaching_note: Microeconomics studies individual units (household/firm); macroeconomics is the AGGREGATE of millions of micro decisions, summed over space (geography/sector) and time (quarter/year). Markets do the aggregating; macro variables emerge from it.

distractors.wrong: Macro studies a single firm's pricing
distractors.why: that is microeconomics; macro is the economy-wide aggregate

nodes.sample_question: What does it mean that macro variables are 'aggregated over space and time'?
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking macro is just 'big micro' — it is the emergent aggregate, and individual intuitions can fail at the aggregate level.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Every macro variable carries a dual fingerprint: a QUANTITY and its PRICE. GDP(qty)/inflation(price); money(qty)/interest rate(price); govt budget(qty)/tax rate(price); trade balance(qty)/exchange rate(price); employment(qty)/wage(price); capital(qty)/rental rate(price).

distractors.wrong: Interest rate is the quantity of money
distractors.why: interest rate is the PRICE of money; the quantity is the money stock

nodes.sample_question: Name the quantity that pairs with each price: inflation, interest rate, exchange rate, wage.
nodes.failure_mode: Treating a price variable and its quantity variable as unrelated — they are paired sides of the same market.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Real vs nominal GDP; constant vs current prices
nodes.teaching_note: Nominal GDP values output at CURRENT prices (mixes price + quantity changes); real GDP values it at CONSTANT base-year prices to isolate the quantity story. Because you cannot add apples+oranges, convert to money, then hold prices fixed to a chosen base year (convention: a past year) to measure real growth. The price story separated out is inflation (deflator/index).

distractors.wrong: Nominal GDP holds prices constant
distractors.why: that is REAL GDP; nominal uses current prices

distractors.wrong: If nominal GDP rises 8% and inflation is 6%, real growth is 8%
distractors.why: real ≈ nominal − inflation ≈ 2%

nodes.sample_question: Nominal GDP grew 11% while inflation was 6%. Roughly what was real GDP growth, and why isn't it 11%?
nodes.failure_mode: Reading nominal growth as real growth — nominal change conflates price inflation with real output change.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Short-run vs long-run: trend vs fluctuations
nodes.teaching_note: GDP = a smooth upward LONG-RUN trend (supply-driven, ~10yr) + SHORT-RUN zigzag fluctuations around it (demand-driven, ~1yr). In the long run all factors are flexible; in the short run they are sticky/fixed. THE organizing distinction of the course — the same shock can have opposite SR vs LR effects.

distractors.wrong: The long run is demand-driven, the short run supply-driven
distractors.why: reversed — SR is demand-driven, LR supply-driven

distractors.wrong: In the short run all prices/wages are fully flexible
distractors.why: they are STICKY in the short run; flexible only in the long run

nodes.sample_question: Why is the short run 'demand-driven' but the long run 'supply-driven'? Give the intuition.
nodes.failure_mode: Applying a short-run mechanism to a long-run question (or vice-versa). Always fix the timeframe first.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Short-run fluctuations come partly from SHOCKS — surprises hitting demand (consumption/investment/export demand), supply (oil prices, pandemic production halt, monsoon), or policy (visa/tariff rules). A shock can morph (COVID: health→supply→demand). They arrive staggered and distributed, not as one instantaneous hit.

distractors.wrong: An oil-price spike is a demand shock
distractors.why: it raises production costs → supply (cost-push) shock

distractors.wrong: Shocks always hit instantaneously and all at once
distractors.why: they are staggered and distributed over time

nodes.sample_question: Classify: (a) global oil-price spike, (b) central bank cuts rates spurring home loans, (c) pandemic lockdown.
nodes.failure_mode: Mislabeling a shock's origin — e.g. calling an oil-price spike a demand shock; it is a cost-push supply shock.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Frictions: price stickiness, info asymmetry, credit constraints
nodes.teaching_note: The economy is choppy in the SR because it is not a frictionless machine: prices are STICKY (menu costs — Domino's can't reprint menus daily; wage contracts fixed for a year), information is asymmetric, and credit/liquidity is constrained. Frictions vanish in the long run when everything adjusts.

distractors.wrong: Menu costs mean prices adjust instantly to shocks
distractors.why: menu costs are precisely why prices are STICKY/slow

distractors.wrong: Frictions operate mainly in the long run
distractors.why: they are short-run; the long run is frictionless/flexible

nodes.sample_question: Define price stickiness ('menu costs') and explain why it makes the short-run economy choppy.
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming instant adjustment — frictions are why short-run effects lag and persist.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Households and firms transact in two markets: the RESOURCE market (households supply labour, firms pay wages) and the PRODUCT market (firms sell goods, households spend). Real flows (goods, labour) run opposite to nominal flows (money). Government taxes both and provides public goods. One agent's spending is another's income — the basis for measuring GDP.

distractors.wrong: Money and goods flow in the same direction
distractors.why: they flow in opposite directions in the circular flow

nodes.sample_question: In the circular flow, which direction does money flow relative to goods/labour, and why?
nodes.failure_mode: Forgetting that money and real goods flow in OPPOSITE directions around the loop.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Dip the 'thermometer' anywhere in the circular flow and (in principle) get the same reading: PRODUCTION (count output) = EXPENDITURE (count spending) = INCOME (count earnings), because one person's spending is another's income. Conceptually equal; the EXPENDITURE approach is most practical to execute.

distractors.wrong: The income approach normally yields a larger GDP than the expenditure approach
distractors.why: conceptually they are equal; differences are only measurement error

distractors.wrong: Production approach is the easiest to implement
distractors.why: expenditure is the most practical; income/production are harder

nodes.sample_question: Why are the production, expenditure and income approaches to GDP conceptually identical?
nodes.failure_mode: Believing the three approaches give different GDP figures conceptually — they measure the same flow at different points.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: GDP identity: Y = C + I + G + NX
nodes.formula: Y = C + I + G + NX, where NX = Exports − Imports
nodes.teaching_note: From the expenditure approach: everything produced-at-home + imported = everything consumed + invested + bought by govt + exported. Rearranged: Y = C + I + G + (Ex − Im) = C + I + G + NX. An accounting IDENTITY, true by construction. NX can be negative (trade deficit).

distractors.wrong: Y = C + I + G + Im (imports added)
distractors.why: imports are SUBTRACTED: NX = Ex − Im

distractors.wrong: A rise in imports, all else equal, raises GDP
distractors.why: imports enter NX negatively → reduce measured GDP

nodes.sample_question: Using Y=C+I+G+NX, what happens to GDP if exports rise while imports are unchanged?
nodes.failure_mode: Adding imports with a + sign, or forgetting NX = exports − imports (net).

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Rearranging the GDP identity with taxes T: private savings (Y−C−T) + public savings (T−G) + foreign savings (Im−Ex) = Investment (I). Total savings (private+public+foreign) must equal investment — an accounting identity, not a behavioural claim.

distractors.wrong: A government deficit (T<G) has no link to private/foreign saving
distractors.why: it must be offset by higher private or foreign saving (lower I) by identity

distractors.wrong: Savings and investment are unrelated quantities
distractors.why: they are equal by the national-accounts identity

nodes.sample_question: If the government runs a deficit (T<G) and private saving is unchanged, what must adjust to keep S=I?
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing 'saving' (the act) with 'investment' (capital formation), or forgetting the foreign-savings term in an open economy.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Dividing the identity by Y gives C/Y + I/Y + G/Y + NX/Y = 100%; the evolving shares tell a country's story (India post-1991 liberalization: imports/exports & investment up, consumption share down; China export/investment-driven; US consumption-driven). Per-capita GDP (GDP/population) proxies living standards better than aggregate GDP.

distractors.wrong: Aggregate GDP measures standard of living
distractors.why: per-capita GDP does; a populous country can have high GDP but low per-capita

nodes.sample_question: Why do economists prefer per-capita GDP over aggregate GDP to compare living standards?
nodes.failure_mode: Reading aggregate GDP as living standards — per-capita GDP is the right comparator across countries.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Money is anything serving as (1) MEDIUM OF EXCHANGE, (2) UNIT OF ACCOUNT, and (3) STORE OF VALUE. Good money also needs legality, acceptability, reasonably stable value (low inflation), and network effects.

distractors.wrong: A primary function of money is to generate interest income
distractors.why: that is not a function of money itself; the three are exchange, account, store of value

nodes.sample_question: State the three functions of money and which one inflation most directly erodes.
nodes.failure_mode: Listing only 'medium of exchange' and missing unit-of-account / store-of-value.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Money is debt; central-bank vs commercial-bank money
nodes.teaching_note: Fiat currency is an IOU: a ₹500 note is the RBI Governor's promise (a central-bank liability), not backed by gold (since 1971). Bank DEPOSITS are IOUs of COMMERCIAL banks, not the central bank. In India only ~3-5% of money is cash (central-bank money); ~95% is deposits (commercial-bank money). Both circulate but are different promises with different risk.

distractors.wrong: Indian fiat currency is backed by gold
distractors.why: fiat is NOT gold-backed (since the early 1970s); it's a central-bank promise

distractors.wrong: Bank deposits are direct liabilities of the central bank
distractors.why: they are commercial-bank IOUs, not central-bank money

nodes.sample_question: A ₹500 note and ₹500 in your savings account — whose liability is each, and which is 'central-bank money'?
nodes.failure_mode: Treating cash and bank deposits as the same kind of money — they are liabilities of different issuers.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: M0 / high-powered / base money = currency with public + banks' reserves at the central bank (purest central-bank money). M1 (narrow money) = currency + demand deposits — spendable immediately. M3 (broad money, India's headline) = narrow money + time deposits (FDs). Broad ⊃ narrow ⊃ base.

distractors.wrong: M0 (base money) is larger than M3 (broad money)
distractors.why: M3 is much larger; base money is multiplied up into broad money

distractors.wrong: Time deposits (FDs) are part of narrow money M1
distractors.why: they are in BROAD money; M1 is currency + demand deposits

nodes.sample_question: Rank M0, M1, M3 by size and state what each adds over the previous.
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing base money (M0, central-bank-created) with broad money (M3, mostly bank-created via the multiplier).

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: OUTSIDE money is created by the government/central bank from outside the private system (currency, reserves) — it is net positive wealth to the private sector. INSIDE money is created within the private banking system (deposits); every deposit-asset is matched by a loan-liability, so inside money nets to zero for the private sector as a whole.

distractors.wrong: Inside money (bank deposits) is net positive wealth for the private sector
distractors.why: it nets to zero — each deposit is matched by a loan; only OUTSIDE money is net positive

nodes.sample_question: Why is 'inside money' said to net to zero for the private sector while 'outside money' does not?
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking commercial banks create net new wealth — inside money is matched by offsetting liabilities (nets to zero).

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.formula: Money multiplier = 1 / CRR;  Total deposits = Base money × (1/CRR)
nodes.teaching_note: Banks keep a fraction (cash reserve ratio, CRR) of deposits and lend the rest; the loan becomes a new deposit elsewhere, cascading. Total deposits / base money = 1/CRR. India CRR ~4-5% → multiplier ~20-25. Cutting CRR raises the multiplier and credit (post-demonetisation: CRR cut released ~₹1.5tn of lending capacity).

distractors.wrong: Raising the CRR increases the money multiplier
distractors.why: a higher CRR LOWERS the multiplier (1/CRR), shrinking money creation

distractors.wrong: With CRR = 5%, the multiplier is 5

nodes.sample_question: If the RBI cuts CRR from 5% to 4%, how does the money multiplier change (give both values)?
nodes.failure_mode: Forgetting the multiplier is 1/CRR — a lower CRR means a LARGER multiplier and more money creation.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Government bonds: face value, coupon, maturity
nodes.teaching_note: A government bond (G-Sec) is a written promise to repay a FACE VALUE at MATURITY plus a fixed COUPON (interest) each period. The coupon is fixed and printed on the bond; it does not change. Short-maturity govt paper = T-bills; longer = notes/bonds. The safest rupee instrument (sovereign promise).

distractors.wrong: A bond's coupon changes as its market price changes
distractors.why: the coupon is fixed/printed; the YIELD changes with price

nodes.sample_question: A ₹100 face-value bond has a 6.5% coupon. What rupee interest does it pay yearly, and does that change if its price falls?
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing the fixed coupon rate with the yield (the coupon never changes; the yield does).

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Bond yield and price move inversely
nodes.formula: Current yield = annual coupon (₹) / current price (₹)
nodes.teaching_note: Yield = fixed coupon ÷ current price. Since the coupon is fixed, when a bond's PRICE rises the YIELD falls, and vice-versa. E.g. ₹10 coupon: at price ₹100 → 10% yield; at ₹90 → 11.1%; at ₹110 → 9.1%. Yields (not coupons) are the market 'interest rates' economists track.

distractors.wrong: When bond prices rise, yields also rise
distractors.why: they move INVERSELY — price up, yield down

distractors.wrong: A ₹10-coupon bond bought at ₹90 yields 10%
distractors.why: 10/90 ≈ 11.1%, above the 10% coupon

nodes.sample_question: A bond pays a fixed ₹10/yr. Its price falls from ₹100 to ₹80. What happens to its yield (compute)?
nodes.failure_mode: Getting the direction wrong — a price RISE means a yield FALL (inverse relationship).

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Interest rate = price of money over time
nodes.teaching_note: The interest rate is the RENT on money — the price of borrowing today, compensating the lender's opportunity cost and the cost of waiting. Normally positive (people must be paid to defer consumption); can be ~0 (Japan 1990s) or even negative in rare crises (Switzerland/Denmark 2015-20).

distractors.wrong: Interest rates can never be zero or negative
distractors.why: rare but real: Japan ~0%, Switzerland/Denmark went negative

nodes.sample_question: Explain why interest rates are normally positive, in terms of waiting and opportunity cost.
nodes.failure_mode: Treating interest as a fee unrelated to time — it is fundamentally the price of money ACROSS time.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Repo rate as policy anchor; arbitrage transmission
nodes.teaching_note: The RBI sets one POLICY rate — the repo rate (rate at which it lends overnight to banks against govt-bond collateral, 'repurchase obligation'). It doesn't set every rate; via an ARBITRAGE mechanism (connected-water-tanks analogy) all other rates in the family adjust around the repo anchor. 'RBI wags the dog; the whole ecosystem follows.'

distractors.wrong: The RBI directly fixes home-loan and deposit rates
distractors.why: it sets only the policy (repo) rate; other rates adjust by arbitrage

distractors.wrong: Repo lending is unsecured
distractors.why: it is secured against government-bond collateral

nodes.sample_question: The RBI raises the repo rate by 50bps. Explain how home-loan rates end up rising without the RBI setting them directly.
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking the RBI directly sets all interest rates — it sets the anchor; markets transmit it via arbitrage.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Inflation; CPI vs WPI; headline vs core
nodes.teaching_note: Inflation = sustained rise in the general price level, measured by tracking a fixed basket. WPI tracks wholesale/production-side prices; CPI tracks consumer-side prices (food, fuel, housing…). HEADLINE CPI includes volatile food & fuel; CORE inflation = CPI minus food & fuel (persistent, sticky — a diagnostic). India's RBI targets headline CPI.

distractors.wrong: Core inflation includes food and fuel
distractors.why: core EXCLUDES food & fuel; headline includes them

distractors.wrong: The RBI's inflation target is WPI
distractors.why: India targets CPI (headline)

nodes.sample_question: Define core inflation and explain why a central bank watches it even though it targets headline CPI.
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing headline (volatile, food+fuel) with core (persistent) — and forgetting the RBI targets headline CPI.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: DEMAND-PULL inflation: excess demand bids prices up (queue at the pizza shop) — the RBI CAN fight it by raising rates to curb borrowing/spending. COST-PUSH inflation: supply-side cost shocks (oil, monsoon, war) push prices up — the RBI is largely helpless (raising rates can't grow tomatoes). Diagnosing the source determines whether monetary policy can help.

distractors.wrong: The RBI can cure an oil-price-driven inflation by raising rates
distractors.why: that's cost-push; rate hikes curb demand, not supply shocks

distractors.wrong: Demand-pull and cost-push call for the same policy response
distractors.why: they don't — only demand-pull is squarely addressable by monetary policy

nodes.sample_question: Inflation jumps because of a global oil-price spike. Should the RBI raise rates? Why or why not?
nodes.failure_mode: Prescribing rate hikes for cost-push (supply) inflation — monetary policy mainly addresses demand-pull.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Expectations are a third inflation channel and are self-fulfilling: if consumers/firms expect higher inflation they buy/raise prices now, validating it; if they trust low inflation, behaviour stays calm. Central-bank CREDIBILITY anchors expectations — the key reason inflation targeting works.

distractors.wrong: Inflation expectations are irrelevant if there's no real shock
distractors.why: expectations are self-fulfilling and can drive inflation on their own

nodes.sample_question: Explain how an expectation of higher future inflation can become self-fulfilling on both the consumer and firm side.
nodes.failure_mode: Ignoring expectations — even without a real shock, expected inflation can become actual inflation.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Since the 2016 RBI Act amendment, the RBI has a legal mandate to keep CPI inflation at 4% within a ±2% band (2–6%), set by a Monetary Policy Committee. If inflation stays outside 2–6% for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must report to government (accountability). 'Flexible' = a band over time, not a point.

distractors.wrong: India targets exactly 4% with no tolerance band
distractors.why: it's 4% ± 2% (a 2–6% band)

distractors.wrong: The target is enforced on WPI
distractors.why: it is CPI (headline)

nodes.sample_question: State India's inflation target and the accountability trigger if the RBI persistently misses it.
nodes.failure_mode: Stating a single point target (4%) without the ±2% band, or attributing it to WPI.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.formula: Output gap = Actual GDP − Potential GDP
nodes.teaching_note: Output gap = actual GDP − potential GDP. NEGATIVE gap: economy below capacity → slack, idle factories, unemployment. POSITIVE gap: producing above sustainable capacity → overheating → inflation (like cramming by cutting sleep — unsustainable). The RBI wants the gap near zero.

distractors.wrong: A positive output gap is purely good (more output)
distractors.why: it's unsustainable → inflationary overheating

distractors.wrong: A negative output gap causes inflation
distractors.why: a negative gap causes slack/unemployment; a POSITIVE gap is inflationary

nodes.sample_question: An economy produces above its potential capacity. What is the sign of the output gap and what does it imply for inflation?
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking a positive output gap is unambiguously good — it signals unsustainable overheating/inflation.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Legally the RBI is accountable only for INFLATION (post-2016), but it traditionally also cares about OUTPUT/growth, financial stability and smoothing cycles. The two goals conflict in the short run (fighting inflation can slow growth), making the RBI's job a tug-of-war.

distractors.wrong: The RBI has a legal mandate for both growth and inflation
distractors.why: the LEGAL mandate is inflation; growth is a traditional (non-statutory) objective

nodes.sample_question: What is the RBI's legal mandate vs its traditional objectives, and why do they conflict short-run?
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming the RBI optimizes growth and inflation independently — short-run they trade off.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Car analogy: rates are the accelerator, output the speed, inflation the engine heat. Cutting rates → more borrowing/spending → faster growth BUT overheating/inflation. Raising rates → cools inflation BUT slows growth. This SR trade-off exists because capacity is fixed short-run; in the long run capacity can expand and the trade-off dissolves.

distractors.wrong: Lowering interest rates reduces both inflation and boosts growth
distractors.why: lower rates boost growth but RAISE inflation — that's the trade-off

distractors.wrong: The inflation-output trade-off holds in the long run
distractors.why: it's a SHORT-RUN trade-off; long-run capacity expansion dissolves it

nodes.sample_question: The RBI cuts rates to boost growth. Trace the effect on inflation and explain the short-run trade-off.
nodes.failure_mode: Believing you can raise growth and cut inflation simultaneously in the short run — they trade off.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Auditorium analogy: seats (capacity) are fixed short-run; attendance (output) is set by DEMAND for the speaker. So short-run, the economy produces what people WANT (demand); long-run, it produces what it CAN (supply capacity). This is why the RBI manages demand to keep output near capacity.

distractors.wrong: Short-run output is set by supply capacity
distractors.why: short-run it's DEMAND-determined; supply capacity binds in the long run

nodes.sample_question: Why does the 'auditorium' analogy show short-run output is demand-driven while long-run is supply-driven?
nodes.failure_mode: Applying long-run supply logic to short-run questions — short-run output follows demand.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Monetary transmission: rates → borrowing → C+I → AD
nodes.formula: ↑ repo → ↑ borrowing cost → ↓ C, ↓ I → ↓ AD → ↓ output & inflation (with lags)
nodes.teaching_note: Closed-economy aggregate demand = C + I + G. Both C (EMIs, credit-card spend) and I (firm investment) are partly borrowing-financed, so they depend on interest rates. CHAIN: RBI raises repo → borrowing dearer → C and I fall → aggregate demand falls → output and inflation cool (with lags). Rate cut runs the chain in reverse. Effects lag and depend on interest-elasticity.

distractors.wrong: A repo-rate hike raises consumption and investment demand
distractors.why: it RAISES borrowing cost → LOWERS C and I

distractors.wrong: Monetary policy affects demand instantly
distractors.why: it works with lags (EMIs, habits, contracts adjust slowly)

nodes.sample_question: Walk the full causal chain from an RBI repo-rate CUT to its effect on output and inflation.
nodes.failure_mode: Getting the causal DIRECTION wrong (the core MACRO failure mode): rate HIKE → demand DOWN, not up.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Monetary policy is not omnipotent. (1) It cannot fix COST-PUSH/supply inflation — raising rates curbs demand, not supply ('can't plant tomatoes or drill oil'). Russia-Ukraine 2022: oil ~$90→$130, India CPI >7% (food is ~40-45% of the CPI basket, fuel ~8-10%); aggressive RBI hikes barely dented it because the cause was global supply, not domestic demand → risk of STAGFLATION (high inflation + low growth). (2) The ZERO LOWER BOUND: once rates ≈0 the RBI is 'out of ammunition' (Japan's lost decade — rates cut 6%→~0% by 1995, recession persisted), forcing non-traditional QUANTITATIVE EASING (central bank buys assets to inject liquidity — powerful but risks asset bubbles & currency depreciation). (3) Lags & impaired banks also weaken it.

distractors.wrong: The RBI can cure oil/food-driven (supply) inflation by hiking rates
distractors.why: rate hikes curb demand, not supply; that's the cost-push limit → stagflation risk

distractors.wrong: At the zero lower bound, conventional rate cuts still work fine
distractors.why: below ~0 the RBI loses its main tool and must resort to QE

nodes.sample_question: Inflation hits 7% from a global oil shock. The RBI hikes aggressively but inflation barely falls while growth slows. Name this outcome and explain why monetary policy underperformed.
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming the RBI can always hit its target quickly — lags, the zero bound, and supply shocks limit it.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Yield curve & the family of rates
nodes.teaching_note: The yield curve plots yield vs maturity. It is normally UPWARD-sloping because longer maturities carry a TERM PREMIUM (compensation for locking money up longer / more uncertainty): 10yr yield ≈ short-rate + term premium. Other issuers stack ABOVE the Govt-of-India curve by added risk — state bonds (SDLs) add credit risk; corporate bonds (AAA→AA→BBB→junk) add credit + LIQUIDITY risk. The RBI sets only the short end (repo); via arbitrage the whole curve moves. An INVERTED curve (short yields > long yields) historically signals an impending recession.

distractors.wrong: An inverted yield curve signals a coming boom
distractors.why: it classically signals a recession

distractors.wrong: Corporate and government bonds of equal maturity carry the same yield
distractors.why: corporates sit above GoI by credit + liquidity risk premia

nodes.sample_question: Why is the yield curve usually upward-sloping, and what does an inversion (short > long yields) historically warn of?
nodes.failure_mode: Reading any single rate in isolation — rates form a term-structure family anchored to policy.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Banks are the main conduit of policy and are actively regulated by the RBI via 'knobs': CRR (cash reserve ratio — deposits held as reserves at the RBI, ~4.5%, non-lendable), SLR (statutory liquidity ratio — a fraction of deposits held in govt securities, ~18%), and the capital adequacy ratio (capital to absorb losses). India's system mixes large public-sector banks (>50% of assets), more-efficient private banks (~30-35%), and niche foreign banks (<10%). Banks are NOT passive pipes — their risk appetite and balance-sheet health decide whether RBI rate changes actually reach borrowers.

distractors.wrong: CRR and SLR are the same requirement
distractors.why: CRR is cash reserves at the RBI; SLR is govt-securities holdings

distractors.wrong: Banks mechanically pass through every RBI rate change
distractors.why: banks are active; risk perception & balance-sheet health can block transmission

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish CRR from SLR, and explain why a well-capitalised banking system is needed for monetary policy to reach the real economy.
nodes.failure_mode: Ignoring the banking channel — if intermediation is impaired, rate cuts don't reach borrowers.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.formula: Invest if expected project return > cost of borrowing
nodes.teaching_note: Investment demand is MORE interest-rate-sensitive than consumption, because most investment is debt-financed and is a cost-benefit call: a firm invests only if expected return > borrowing cost. A project returning 12% is viable at an 8% borrowing cost (4% margin) but is shelved if rates rise to 10% (2% margin). In India a ~1% rate cut raises investment ~2%, fastest in the SME/bank-loan segment; the full effect lags ~2-3 months due to approval/contract frictions.

distractors.wrong: Consumption is more interest-rate-sensitive than investment
distractors.why: investment is more sensitive — it's largely debt-financed and margin-driven

distractors.wrong: A rate hike from 8% to 10% leaves a 12%-return project equally attractive
distractors.why: the margin shrinks from 4% to 2%, often shelving the project

nodes.sample_question: A project yields 12%. Borrowing cost rises from 8% to 11%. What happens to the firm's investment decision and why is investment so rate-sensitive?
nodes.failure_mode: Treating investment as rate-insensitive — it is the MOST rate-sensitive demand component.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Monetary policy is a 'Swiss-army knife' transmitting through FIVE channels, not one: (1) INTEREST-RATE channel (repo→loan rates→C and I); (2) BANK-CREDIT channel (more liquidity / lower CRR → banks relax lending standards & approve more loans); (3) BALANCE-SHEET channel (lower rates lift borrowers' asset/collateral values → they look safer → easier credit); (4) ASSET-PRICE channel (cheap liquidity lifts stocks & real estate → WEALTH EFFECT → more spending; firms also raise equity cheaply via IPOs — vivid in COVID); (5) EXPECTATIONS channel (an accommodative signal shifts beliefs → households/firms spend & invest now, self-fulfilling).

distractors.wrong: Monetary policy works only through the interest-rate channel
distractors.why: there are five: interest-rate, credit, balance-sheet, asset-price, expectations

distractors.wrong: The 'wealth effect' is part of the bank-credit channel
distractors.why: it is the ASSET-PRICE channel — rising asset values make people feel richer and spend

nodes.sample_question: Name the five channels of monetary-policy transmission and give the one-line mechanism of the asset-price channel.
nodes.failure_mode: Reducing monetary policy to the interest-rate channel alone — four other channels operate in parallel.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Real vs nominal interest rates (Fisher identity)
nodes.formula: Real rate ≈ Nominal rate − Inflation  (Fisher identity)
nodes.teaching_note: Every quoted rate (repo, loan, deposit, bond yield) is NOMINAL; economic decisions hinge on the REAL rate = nominal − inflation (Fisher identity). A 7% loan with 6% inflation is only ~1% real cost (nearly free); a 6% loan with 6% inflation is a 0% real cost. The RBI sets the nominal rate; the real rate is deduced and is the true economic cost of borrowing.

distractors.wrong: A 7% loan is expensive regardless of inflation
distractors.why: at 6% inflation its REAL cost is only ~1%

distractors.wrong: The RBI directly sets the real interest rate
distractors.why: the RBI sets the NOMINAL rate; the real rate is nominal − inflation

nodes.sample_question: A firm borrows at 8% when inflation is 7%. What is the approximate real interest rate, and why does it matter more than the nominal rate?
nodes.failure_mode: Judging borrowing cost by the nominal rate, ignoring that inflation erodes it (real = nominal − inflation).

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: RBI's liquidity toolkit: repo ops, OMO, CRR, SLR, forward guidance
nodes.teaching_note: Beyond setting the repo rate the RBI manages money with: REPO/REVERSE-REPO daily ops (lend/absorb overnight vs collateral — fine-tunes the rate; the corridor: MSF = repo+δ, SDF/reverse-repo = repo−δ); OPEN MARKET OPERATIONS (OMO — buying govt bonds PERMANENTLY injects liquidity/expands money, selling withdraws it — a structured permanent tool, unlike the reversible repo); the CRR (reserve ratio — small changes hit hard via the 1/CRR multiplier: COVID cut 4→3% released ~₹1.75tn; demonetisation 4.75→4% released ~₹1.5tn); the SLR; and FORWARD GUIDANCE (communicating the future rate-path stance — dovish/accommodative, neutral, or hawkish — which moves markets WITHOUT touching the repo, vital at the zero lower bound).

distractors.wrong: OMO and repo operations are both temporary/reversible
distractors.why: repo is reversible (repurchase); OMO is a PERMANENT injection/withdrawal

distractors.wrong: Forward guidance requires changing the repo rate
distractors.why: it moves markets purely via communication of the future stance

nodes.sample_question: Contrast a repo operation with an open-market operation (OMO) in terms of permanence, and explain how forward guidance moves markets without a rate change.
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking the repo rate is the RBI's only tool — OMO, CRR and forward guidance are distinct, powerful levers.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Transmission can break INSIDE the financial system. NPAs (non-performing assets — loans unpaid >90 days) force banks to set aside PROVISIONS, eroding lending capital → banks turn risk-averse and fail to pass on RBI rate cuts (India's public-sector banks, 2014-19). NBFCs (non-bank financial companies, ~20% of credit — 'shadow banking') lend like banks but cannot take deposits, so they borrow SHORT (markets/banks) and lend LONG — structurally fragile. The IL&FS default (2018, ~₹90,000cr) triggered CONTAGION: ratings downgrades → credit freeze → SMEs/auto/housing borrowers cut off — showing the system's upstream-downstream linkages.

distractors.wrong: High NPAs make banks lend more freely
distractors.why: provisions erode capital → banks turn risk-averse and lend less

distractors.wrong: NBFCs fund themselves with public deposits like banks
distractors.why: they CANNOT take deposits; they borrow short from markets/banks — hence fragility

nodes.sample_question: Why did high public-sector-bank NPAs (2014-19) blunt RBI rate cuts, and why are deposit-less NBFCs structurally fragile?
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming RBI rate cuts always reach borrowers — NPAs and NBFC stress can freeze transmission.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.formula: Y = C + I + G + NX;  NX = Exports − Imports
nodes.teaching_note: Opening the economy adds NET EXPORTS: Y = C + I + G + NX, NX = Exports − Imports (the 'trade balance'). NX>0 = trade surplus (net seller; foreign demand ADDS to GDP); NX<0 = trade deficit (net buyer; domestic demand leaks abroad). EXPORTS depend on (i) global/world income, (ii) the real exchange rate, (iii) trade barriers/tariffs. IMPORTS depend on (i) domestic income, (ii) the real exchange rate, (iii) tariffs. So a rupee depreciation raises exports & cuts imports (improving NX); a domestic boom raises imports (worsening NX).

distractors.wrong: A domestic boom (rising domestic income) improves the trade balance
distractors.why: it raises IMPORTS → worsens NX

distractors.wrong: Rising imports increase GDP via the identity
distractors.why: imports enter NX negatively → reduce measured GDP

nodes.sample_question: India's exports rise (imports unchanged). What happens to GDP via Y=C+I+G+NX? And what happens to NX if instead domestic income booms?
nodes.failure_mode: Directional error — thinking higher imports raise GDP, or that a domestic boom improves the trade balance.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Exchange rate in the asset market
nodes.formula: E = rupees per $1;  rupee 'price' = 1/E;  E↑ ⇒ $ appreciates, ₹ depreciates
nodes.teaching_note: Treat currencies as commodities. The NOMINAL exchange rate E = price of $1 in rupees (E=90 ⇒ ₹90 per $). If E rises the dollar APPRECIATES and the rupee DEPRECIATES (rupee price is the inverse, 1/E). More rupees chasing dollars → dollar dearer. To price E, set up a US investor with D dollars and a no-arbitrage choice: (a) US bond → (1+i_US)·D; or (b) convert to rupees at E_today, buy the Indian bond, reconvert at E_tomorrow → (1+i_IND)·D·(E_today/E_tomorrow). Arbitrage equalises the two routes — this yields interest-rate parity.

distractors.wrong: If E rises from 80 to 90, the rupee has appreciated
distractors.why: E↑ = rupee DEPRECIATION (you pay more ₹ per $)

nodes.sample_question: The exchange rate moves from ₹80/$ to ₹90/$. Which currency appreciated, and set up the US investor's two no-arbitrage routes.
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing the direction: E↑ means rupee DEPRECIATION (dollar appreciation), not strengthening.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.formula: UIP: %ΔE (₹ depreciation) ≈ i_IND − i_US;  Covered IRP uses the forward rate to lock E
nodes.teaching_note: UNCOVERED interest parity (UIP), from no-arbitrage: E_tomorrow/E_today = (1+i_IND)/(1+i_US); linearised, the expected % depreciation of the rupee ≈ i_IND − i_US (interest-rate differential). Empirically UIP fits POORLY period-to-period (currency risk isn't hedged), but the LONG-RUN average holds: India ~7% vs US ~3% ⇒ ~4%/yr differential, and the rupee depreciated ~4%/yr (₹65/$ in 2015 → ₹90/$ in 2025, ≈40% over 10 yrs). COVERED interest parity — locking the future rate with an FX forward/future — removes the exchange risk and matches data much better.

distractors.wrong: UIP says a higher domestic interest rate makes the currency appreciate over time
distractors.why: UIP implies expected DEPRECIATION ≈ the rate differential

distractors.wrong: Uncovered IRP fits the data better than covered IRP
distractors.why: covered IRP (hedged with forwards) fits much better

nodes.sample_question: India's bond yield is 7%, the US's is 3%. By UIP, what is the expected annual change in the ₹/$ rate, and in which direction?
nodes.failure_mode: Mixing the direction — a HIGHER domestic rate is matched by EXPECTED DEPRECIATION, not appreciation, under UIP.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Exchange rate in the product market (PPP)
nodes.formula: Real exchange rate e = E·(P_US / P_India);  long-run PPP: e → 1
nodes.teaching_note: From the product market: the REAL exchange rate e = E·(P_US/P_India) — how many Indian goods one US good buys after conversion (the Big Mac index makes it concrete: a US Big Mac that buys 2 Indian Big Macs ⇒ e≈2). PURCHASING POWER PARITY says arbitrage drives identical tradable goods to the same price, so in the LONG RUN e → 1 (a gravitational anchor). e>1 ⇒ domestic goods are cheap / currency UNDERvalued ⇒ demand for rupees rises ⇒ rupee tends to APPRECIATE toward 1; e<1 ⇒ OVERvalued ⇒ tends to depreciate. Short-run e moves mainly through the fast-moving nominal rate E (prices P are sticky).

distractors.wrong: A real exchange rate above 1 means the currency is overvalued and will depreciate
distractors.why: e>1 ⇒ goods cheap ⇒ UNDERvalued ⇒ tends to APPRECIATE toward 1

distractors.wrong: PPP holds tightly month-to-month
distractors.why: PPP is a LONG-RUN anchor; short-run e floats around 1 via the nominal rate

nodes.sample_question: A US Big Mac converts to enough rupees to buy 2 Indian Big Macs (e≈2). Is the rupee over- or under-valued, and which way does PPP push it?
nodes.failure_mode: Applying PPP to short-run moves (it's a long-run anchor) or mixing under/over-valuation directions.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Three desirables — (1) a FIXED exchange rate (certainty), (2) free CAPITAL MOBILITY (efficient global allocation), (3) INDEPENDENT monetary policy (sovereignty) — but only TWO can hold at once (the trilemma). It falls straight out of UIP: fix E (ratio=1) + free mobility (the arbitrage '=' holds) forces i_IND = i_US, killing independence. Choices: Eurozone & Hong Kong/Saudi/Qatar = fixed + mobility (give up independence); China = fixed + independence (capital controls); US/UK = floating + mobility + independence (give up the fix). It's a SPECTRUM, not all-or-nothing: India sits in the middle (managed float + partial capital controls + semi-independent policy), getting partial benefits of all three.

distractors.wrong: With free capital mobility and a fixed exchange rate, a country still keeps independent monetary policy
distractors.why: UIP forces i_domestic = i_foreign — independence is lost

distractors.wrong: The trilemma is an all-or-nothing choice among the three corners
distractors.why: it's a spectrum; most countries (incl. India) sit in the middle

nodes.sample_question: India fixes the rupee AND keeps open capital flows. Show via UIP why it then cannot set its interest rate independently.
nodes.failure_mode: Claiming all three can hold simultaneously, or that the choice is binary rather than a spectrum.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Exchange-rate regimes; nominal vs real shocks
nodes.teaching_note: Regimes span FIXED (a peg, e.g. Hong Kong→USD; needs reserves + capital controls) → MANAGED/'dirty' FLOAT (market-determined but the central bank intervenes on volatility — India since the mid-1990s) → FREE FLOAT (pure market, e.g. USD/EUR/JPY). Terminology matters: under floating, currency moves are DEPRECIATION/APPRECIATION (market-driven); under a fix, a deliberate policy move is DEVALUATION/REVALUATION (govt/central-bank decision — e.g. India's 1991 devaluation). The regime choice trades off price certainty against monetary autonomy (per the trilemma).

distractors.wrong: A market-driven fall in a floating currency is called a 'devaluation'
distractors.why: that's DEPRECIATION; devaluation is a deliberate policy cut under a fixed regime

distractors.wrong: India runs a hard fixed-exchange-rate peg
distractors.why: India runs a MANAGED float since the mid-1990s

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish depreciation from devaluation, and classify India's current exchange-rate regime.
nodes.failure_mode: Using 'devaluation' for a market-driven float move (that's depreciation) — devaluation is a policy act under a peg.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.formula: ↑i → capital inflow → ₹ appreciates → exports↓, imports↑ → NX↓ → AD↓ → inflation↓
nodes.teaching_note: A SECOND transmission channel beyond the interest-rate channel. CHAIN: RBI raises rates → (via UIP, with mobile capital) foreign capital flows in chasing higher Indian yields → demand for rupees rises → rupee NOMINALLY appreciates → (prices sticky) REAL appreciation → Indian exports dearer, foreign goods cheaper → exports↓, imports↑ → NX↓ → aggregate demand↓ → inflation↓. Its strength depends on (a) CAPITAL MOBILITY (high mobility → big flows from small rate gaps) and (b) the EXCHANGE-RATE REGIME (blocked under a hard peg, since the RBI must defend the fixed rate; partial under India's managed float).

distractors.wrong: An RBI rate hike depreciates the rupee and boosts exports
distractors.why: a hike attracts capital → rupee APPRECIATES → exports FALL

distractors.wrong: The exchange-rate channel works fully under a hard fixed peg
distractors.why: under a peg the RBI must defend the rate, blocking the channel

nodes.sample_question: Trace how an RBI rate HIKE affects net exports and inflation through the exchange-rate channel, and state the two conditions it depends on.
nodes.failure_mode: Forgetting this is a distinct channel, or reversing it (a rate HIKE appreciates the rupee and CUTS net exports).

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.formula: Current account + Capital account = 0  (a CAD is financed by a capital-account surplus)
nodes.teaching_note: The Balance of Payments records all transactions with the world over a period. CURRENT account = trade in goods & services + income (dividends) + transfers (NRI remittances); CAPITAL/financial account = FDI, FPI, external commercial borrowings (ECB), and changes in RBI reserves. By double-entry, current + capital = 0: a current-account DEFICIT (imports>exports) MUST be financed by a capital-account surplus (borrowing/selling assets to foreigners). Whether a CAD is 'bad' depends on (1) USE — investment/capital goods (good, like an education loan) vs consumption (bad); (2) SOURCE — patient FDI vs hot-money FPI; (3) SIZE — ~2-2.5% of GDP comfortable, 4-5% danger (India ~1.3%). The 1991 crisis: a Gulf-War oil spike + falling remittances drained reserves to ~$1bn (2 weeks of imports); India airlifted 47t of gold to the Bank of England and launched the reforms.

distractors.wrong: A current-account deficit can exist without any offsetting capital inflow
distractors.why: by the BoP identity it MUST be financed by a capital-account surplus / reserve drawdown

distractors.wrong: A larger current-account deficit is always more dangerous than a smaller one
distractors.why: what it FUNDS (investment vs consumption) and its SOURCE (FDI vs FPI) matter more than size

nodes.sample_question: India runs a $30bn current-account deficit. By the BoP identity how is it financed, and what three questions decide whether it is dangerous?
nodes.failure_mode: Treating the current account in isolation, or judging a deficit by size alone (use & source matter more).

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Currency crises recur when a country holds a (managed/fixed) exchange rate + open capital + dollar-denominated debt, then sentiment reverses — 'hot money' (FPI) flees, reserves run out, the peg breaks, and CONTAGION spreads ('fear travels faster than facts'). Case library: East Asia 1997 (Thai baht peg, China's 1994 devaluation hurt exports → reserves gone → IMF bailout); Mexico 1994 'Tequila' (dollar tesobonos + political shocks); Argentina 2001 (1:1 dollar peg + Brazil's 1999 devaluation); Euro/Greece (gave up monetary independence → only 'internal devaluation'/austerity left); India 2013 TAPER TANTRUM (Fed QE-taper hint → FPI fled → rupee ₹54→₹68, −25% in 3 months); Sri Lanka 2022 (dollar debt + COVID tourism/remittance collapse + fertilizer-import ban → default, ₹200→360); Turkey (Erdogan kept rates low despite inflation → lira crash, ~80% inflation). Lesson: avoid over-reliance on volatile FPI; keep CAD low and reserves high.

distractors.wrong: A country with a hard peg, open capital account and dollar debt is well-insulated from crises
distractors.why: that's exactly the fragile combination that breaks in a sudden capital reversal

distractors.wrong: The 2013 'Taper Tantrum' was caused by an actual RBI policy change
distractors.why: it was triggered by a US Fed signal about tapering QE — a foreign shock

nodes.sample_question: Why did the 2013 'Taper Tantrum' crash the rupee 25%, and what made India structurally vulnerable to it?
nodes.failure_mode: Seeing each crisis as unique rather than the same impossible-trinity + hot-money pattern; underrating contagion.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: History of exchange-rate regimes (gold → Bretton Woods → fiat)
nodes.teaching_note: Regime history: the classical GOLD STANDARD (1870-1914, currencies fixed to gold) → BRETTON WOODS (1944: the US$ fixed to gold at $35/oz, other currencies pegged to the $) → in 1971 President Nixon CLOSED THE GOLD WINDOW (US printed too many dollars financing the Vietnam War; couldn't honour gold), ending Bretton Woods. Since 1971 money is pure FIAT — value rests on TRUST in institutions/policy credibility, not a commodity anchor — and major currencies FLOAT. Developed economies float; emerging economies often run managed floats with capital controls.

distractors.wrong: The rupee is backed by gold reserves at the RBI
distractors.why: since 1971 money is fiat — backed by institutional trust, not gold

distractors.wrong: Bretton Woods established floating exchange rates
distractors.why: it established FIXED rates ($-to-gold); floating came after its 1971 collapse

nodes.sample_question: What did Nixon's 1971 'closing of the gold window' change about what gives money its value?
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking modern currencies are gold-backed — they are fiat (trust-based) since 1971.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Regime choice: nominal vs real shocks
nodes.teaching_note: The economic case for a fixed vs flexible regime depends on the dominant shock. A FIXED rate INSULATES against NOMINAL shocks (monetary/paper shocks) — you don't want the real economy disturbed by a paper wrapper. A FLEXIBLE rate is better for REAL shocks (e.g. an oil discovery, a productivity change) because it lets relative prices/real allocations adjust. Since countries face BOTH, most adopt a MANAGED float (flexibility + intervention) as a compromise.

distractors.wrong: A flexible exchange rate best insulates against nominal (monetary) shocks
distractors.why: a FIXED rate insulates nominal shocks; flexible suits REAL shocks

distractors.wrong: Real shocks call for a fixed exchange rate
distractors.why: real shocks need price/allocation adjustment → FLEXIBLE rate

nodes.sample_question: Should a country facing mainly real (supply-side) shocks prefer a fixed or flexible exchange rate, and why?
nodes.failure_mode: Recommending a fixed rate for real shocks (or floating for nominal shocks) — it's the reverse.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: India's global integration, risk premium & sterilized intervention
nodes.teaching_note: India chose PARTIAL (calibrated) integration. Trade openness ((X+M)/GDP) rose ~15%→~45% (vs China 35-40%, Vietnam/Thailand 120-150%); the capital account is only MODERATELY open (FDI welcomed, short-term debt/FPI restricted). Emerging markets carry a COUNTRY RISK PREMIUM (India ~BBB at S&P vs US AA+, China A+) — when global sentiment turns 'risk-off', capital rushes to US treasuries. The RBI manages rupee VOLATILITY (not a level) via STERILIZED INTERVENTION: it buys/sells dollars, then mops up the resulting rupee liquidity by selling/buying govt bonds, so the exchange-rate action doesn't disturb domestic money/inflation. Plus countercyclical macroprudential tools (variable reserve ratio, ECB caps).

distractors.wrong: 'Sterilized' intervention means the RBI only buys/sells dollars and ignores the rupee-liquidity side-effect
distractors.why: sterilization is the SECOND leg — mopping up rupee liquidity via bond ops so domestic money is unaffected

distractors.wrong: The country risk premium is something the RBI directly controls
distractors.why: it's set by global investors/ratings; the RBI can only manage rates & Forex, not the premium

nodes.sample_question: The RBI buys dollars to stem rupee appreciation. Why must it then sell government bonds, and what is this two-leg operation called?
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking RBI Forex intervention targets a fixed rupee level (it targets volatility) or that it ignores the inflation side-effect (it sterilizes).

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Trade-policy tools shape the quantity/composition of trade beyond monetary policy: TARIFFS (tax on imports — protect domestic/infant industry), IMPORT QUOTAS (cap quantity), EXPORT SUBSIDIES (cheapen exports), NON-TARIFF BARRIERS (standards/licensing), FREE-TRADE AGREEMENTS, and ANTI-DUMPING DUTIES (vs below-cost foreign selling). India's arc: IMPORT-SUBSTITUTION (1950s-80s, ~100% tariffs + licensing → inefficient, slow growth) → 1991 LIBERALIZATION (tariffs ~80%→15%, FTAs, IT/export boom) → mid-2010s STRATEGIC AUTONOMY / Atmanirbhar Bharat (selective tariffs, managed — not full — integration). Tariffs protect visible jobs but invite retaliation and disrupt supply chains (US-China trade war, 'China+1').

distractors.wrong: A tariff is a tax on exports
distractors.why: a tariff is a tax on IMPORTS (to protect domestic producers)

distractors.wrong: India has moved monotonically toward ever-freer trade since independence
distractors.why: it went protectionist (import-substitution) → liberal (1991) → selectively protectionist again (Atmanirbhar)

nodes.sample_question: Define a tariff vs an import quota, and outline the three phases of India's trade-policy evolution.
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming tariffs straightforwardly help — they protect some jobs but trigger retaliation and raise input costs.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Fiscal policy is the finance ministry's use of government SPENDING (the G in Y=C+I+G+NX) and TAXES to manage aggregate demand. Spending injects money into the private economy (highways, salaries); taxes pull money out. Versus monetary policy it is SLOWER (annual budget, not weekly), more TARGETED (you can direct a highway or a cash transfer), and POLITICAL (decided by elected governments, not an independent technocrat).

distractors.wrong: Fiscal policy is faster-acting than monetary policy
distractors.why: fiscal is SLOWER — budget cycles & execution lags; monetary is fast

distractors.wrong: Fiscal policy is set by the RBI
distractors.why: it's the finance ministry; the RBI runs MONETARY policy

nodes.sample_question: Give two ways fiscal policy differs from monetary policy in how it reaches the economy.
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing fiscal (G & taxes, finance ministry) with monetary (rates & money, RBI); calling fiscal policy 'fast'.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Governments fund themselves via (1) TAXES — direct (income/corporate) vs indirect (GST/excise); fund ~60-70% of India's budget; (2) BORROWING (issuing bonds); (3) MONEY CREATION (monetisation — inflationary, avoided in normal years). India also has large NON-TAX revenue (PSU dividends, disinvestment, user fees). Of every ₹100 spent India raises ~55-60 from taxes, ~10-12 non-tax, ~30-35 borrowed. SPENDING splits into REVENUE expenditure (runs the system — salaries, pensions, subsidies; non-productive but not wasteful), CAPITAL expenditure (builds the system — roads, ports; PRODUCTIVE, raises future capacity), and TRANSFERS (balance the system). Quality (productive vs not) matters more than quantity.

distractors.wrong: Revenue expenditure (salaries, subsidies) builds long-run productive capacity
distractors.why: that's CAPITAL expenditure; revenue spending runs the system

distractors.wrong: Monetisation (printing money to fund spending) is India's main funding source
distractors.why: it's avoided in normal years (inflationary); taxes are the main source

nodes.sample_question: Classify as revenue or capital expenditure: (a) teacher salaries, (b) a new metro line, (c) a food subsidy. Which is 'productive'?
nodes.failure_mode: Equating all government spending — capital (productive) vs revenue (non-productive) have very different effects.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.formula: Debt/GDP stabilises when growth g > interest rate r (sustainable); spirals when r > g
nodes.teaching_note: A fiscal DEFICIT = spending > (tax + non-tax) revenue (India ~5-6% of GDP, spiked in COVID); accumulated deficits = DEBT (a stock, measured as debt/GDP). GOOD debt finances productive investment that raises future GDP (infrastructure — like an education loan); BAD debt funds consumption/freebies (no future return). SUSTAINABILITY hinges on growth vs interest: debt/GDP stabilises when growth g > interest rate r on debt, and spirals when r > g. India's nominal GDP growth ~10-12% exceeds bond yields ~7% (g>r → manageable); Greece's r>g (couldn't grow, couldn't print in the euro) → crisis. Japan sustains ~250% debt/GDP because g and confidence hold. So it's not the debt level but the dynamics.

distractors.wrong: Debt is sustainable when the interest rate exceeds the growth rate (r > g)
distractors.why: reversed — g > r is the sustainable condition; r > g spirals

distractors.wrong: A 250%-debt/GDP country must be in crisis
distractors.why: Japan sustains ~250% because g & confidence hold — dynamics, not level, decide

nodes.sample_question: India's nominal growth is ~11% and its bond yield ~7%. Is its debt path sustainable, and what is the general condition?
nodes.failure_mode: Judging debt by its level alone, or getting the sustainability inequality backwards (it's g>r that's safe).

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Crowding out: when the government borrows heavily it competes with the private sector for the LIMITED pool of loanable funds → pushes up interest rates → private INVESTMENT (and rate-sensitive consumption) gets squeezed out, partly offsetting the fiscal stimulus. It is WORST in booms (private sector wants those funds, near full capacity) and MINIMAL in deep recessions (private demand for credit is already dead, so government borrowing displaces little). Doubly bad if government borrows to crowd out productive private investment for non-productive spending.

distractors.wrong: Government borrowing lowers interest rates and boosts private investment
distractors.why: it RAISES rates → crowds OUT private investment

distractors.wrong: Crowding out is most severe during a deep recession
distractors.why: it's WEAKEST in recessions (private credit demand is dead); worst in booms

nodes.sample_question: Why is crowding-out a serious concern when the government borrows in a boom, but a minor one in a deep recession?
nodes.failure_mode: Directional error — thinking government borrowing lowers rates; and ignoring that crowding-out is state-dependent (weak in recession).

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.formula: Fiscal multiplier = 1 / (1 − MPC)   [MPC = marginal propensity to consume]
nodes.teaching_note: One rupee of government spending becomes someone's income; they spend a fraction (the marginal propensity to consume, MPC) which becomes the next person's income, and so on — a geometric series. The fiscal MULTIPLIER = 1/(1−MPC). With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier = 1/(1−0.8) = 5, so ₹1 lakh crore of spending can raise GDP by ~₹5 lakh crore. The multiplier is LARGER in a recession (idle capacity, high MPC) and SMALLER near full employment (where extra demand just raises prices / is crowded out).

distractors.wrong: With MPC = 0.8 the multiplier is 0.8
The multiplier is largest near full employment
distractors.why: it's largest in a recession with slack; smallest near full capacity

nodes.sample_question: If the MPC is 0.75, what is the fiscal multiplier, and is it larger in a boom or a slump?
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming ΔGDP = ΔG one-for-one (ignoring the multiplier), or mis-computing 1/(1−MPC).

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Fiscal vs monetary policy; countercyclical use
nodes.teaching_note: Two stabilisation tools compared: SPEED (monetary fast — rate change in weeks; fiscal slow — budget+execution lags); TARGETING (fiscal targeted to a sector/group; monetary hits the economy uniformly); POLITICS (monetary is independent/technocratic; fiscal is political/electoral); and crowding (fiscal can crowd out private investment; monetary easing encourages it). They are COMPLEMENTS, not substitutes — best when coordinated (RBI cuts + government spends → faster growth). But they can CLASH (India 2013-14: government deficits expansionary while the RBI hiked to fight inflation). The extreme 'coordination' is DEBT MONETISATION (RBI prints to buy government debt) — the ultimate coordination and the ultimate risk to central-bank independence.

distractors.wrong: Monetary policy is the slower, more targeted tool
distractors.why: it's FASTER and more uniform; FISCAL is slower and more targeted

distractors.wrong: Debt monetisation poses no risk to central-bank independence
distractors.why: it's the ultimate risk — politicians effectively control money creation

nodes.sample_question: Contrast fiscal and monetary policy on speed and targeting, and explain how they clashed in India around 2013-14.
nodes.failure_mode: Treating fiscal & monetary as interchangeable, or forgetting they can pull in opposite directions.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Growth theory: Malthusian trap & diminishing returns to capital
nodes.teaching_note: Long-run growth is about GDP PER CAPITA. The MALTHUSIAN trap: with land fixed and population growing geometrically, per-capita resources fall toward subsistence — a doomsday path. The Industrial Revolution ESCAPED it by inventing a new, accumulable resource: MACHINES (capital). But capital faces DIMINISHING RETURNS (the laundromat: the 1st machine is transformational, the 5th sits idle) — so accumulating capital alone cannot grow an economy forever; growth slows as the capital stock deepens (China 10%→5-6%, South Korea, India all decelerated). So capital is not the ultimate engine.

distractors.wrong: Accumulating physical capital can grow an economy indefinitely
distractors.why: diminishing returns to capital make growth slow as the capital stock deepens

distractors.wrong: The Malthusian trap was escaped by adding more farmland
distractors.why: it was escaped by inventing MACHINES (an accumulable resource), not more fixed land

nodes.sample_question: Use the laundromat analogy to explain why a country can't grow forever just by building more factories.
nodes.failure_mode: Believing endless investment in capital sustains growth — diminishing returns cap it.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Since capital hits diminishing returns, sustained long-run growth comes from TECHNOLOGY = IDEAS. Ideas are NON-RIVALROUS: my use of an idea (a washing-machine design, Faraday's law, an Excel formula) doesn't prevent yours, and ideas don't wear out — so, unlike machines, they do NOT face diminishing returns and can lift the whole production function indefinitely. This ties back to Module 1's 'thread of technology'. The open question (R&D incentives, patents, education) is how to PRODUCE more ideas.

distractors.wrong: Technology faces the same diminishing returns as physical capital
distractors.why: ideas are NON-RIVALROUS and don't wear out — they escape diminishing returns

distractors.wrong: An idea, once used by one firm, can't be freely used by another
distractors.why: ideas are non-rivalrous — simultaneous use doesn't deplete them (unlike a machine)

nodes.sample_question: Why does technology (ideas) escape the diminishing returns that limit physical capital? Use the non-rivalry property.
nodes.failure_mode: Attributing long-run per-capita growth to more capital/labour rather than to non-rivalrous ideas/technology.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: First-principles myth-busting: (1) a STRONG currency ≠ a strong economy — the exchange rate is a relative price/unit (Afghani 20/$ vs INR 80/$ is like Celsius vs Fahrenheit; CHANGES matter, not absolute levels); a weak currency can aid exports. (2) Printing rupees WEAKENS, not strengthens, the currency (more rupees chasing the same goods → inflation). (3) A trade/current-account DEFICIT isn't inherently bad — growing economies import capital goods; USE & financing source matter. (4) GDP is a limited measure (ignores distribution & wellbeing). (5) Debt sustainability depends on growth & context (Japan 250% fine; Greece not), not a magic threshold. (6) Markets aggregate information but exhibit fear/greed/herd biases (2008 mispriced risk). Economics is about TRADE-OFFS, not absolutes.

distractors.wrong: A rising rupee (stronger currency) always signals a stronger economy
distractors.why: the level is just a relative price/unit; a weak currency can boost exports — changes, not levels, matter

distractors.wrong: Crossing a 90% debt/GDP ratio mechanically triggers a growth collapse
distractors.why: the Reinhart-Rogoff '90%' threshold was an Excel error; sustainability is context/growth-dependent

nodes.sample_question: 'A strong rupee means a strong India.' Use relative prices and the units argument to explain why this is a myth.
nodes.failure_mode: Reasoning from slogans ('strong rupee = strong India', 'deficits are bad') instead of relative prices & trade-offs.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: Keynes & the birth of fiscal policy
nodes.teaching_note: Before the 1930s the classical view was that markets self-correct, so governments should balance budgets. The Great Depression (1929) — mass unemployment, idle capacity — shattered that. KEYNES argued that in a slump the private sector won't spend, so the GOVERNMENT must spend (even 'dig ditches') to inject demand and pull the economy out of the low-output trap. This founded modern fiscal policy (the US New Deal). Crucially, fiscal policy is the tool of LAST RESORT when monetary policy is exhausted (rates near zero / liquidity trap) — the same logic that returned in COVID-19.

distractors.wrong: Keynes argued governments should balance budgets during a depression
distractors.why: he argued they should SPEND and run deficits to revive demand

distractors.wrong: Fiscal policy is most needed when monetary policy still has room to cut
distractors.why: it's the last resort precisely WHEN monetary policy is exhausted (ZLB)

nodes.sample_question: Why did Keynes argue governments must spend in a depression, and why is fiscal policy the tool of last resort at the zero lower bound?
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming markets always self-correct, or that monetary policy is always available — in a liquidity trap only fiscal works.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Fiscal space = a country's 'credit-card limit' — how much it can borrow before markets stop trusting it. It's larger with low debt/GDP, high growth prospects, a broad tax base, a credible own currency, and strong institutions. The US has vast space (the dollar); India has MODERATE space (debt/GDP ~80-90%, a thin ~17-18% tax base); Sri Lanka had NONE (2022). Fiscal space is dynamic (grows with growth, shrinks with panic). India's FRBM Act (2003) sets discipline anchors — fiscal deficit ~3% of GDP, debt ~60% — with an escape clause (used in COVID); a 'speed limit, not a brick wall'.

distractors.wrong: Every country has the same ability to run large deficits
distractors.why: fiscal space varies hugely (US large via the dollar, Sri Lanka none)

distractors.wrong: The FRBM Act bans all government deficits
distractors.why: it sets disciplinary targets (~3% deficit, ~60% debt) with escape clauses, not a ban

nodes.sample_question: What determines a country's 'fiscal space', and what targets does India's FRBM Act set?
nodes.failure_mode: Treating fiscal space as fixed, or thinking all countries can borrow/spend like the US.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.teaching_note: Fiscal policy should lean AGAINST the cycle: EXPAND (deficits) in recessions, wars, nation-building, or when monetary policy is exhausted; CONTRACT (surpluses) in booms, when inflation is high, or when debt is unsustainable. 'Save in good times, spend in bad' — surpluses in booms, deficits in slumps. Spending in a boom is counterproductive (adds inflation, crowds out a healthy private sector). Cautionary tale: the Reinhart-Rogoff '90% debt/GDP kills growth' threshold that drove global austerity turned out to rest on an EXCEL ERROR (rows omitted) — when fixed, the threshold vanished. No universal rule; context dominates.

distractors.wrong: Governments should increase spending during economic booms
distractors.why: that's procyclical & inflationary; spend in slumps, save in booms

distractors.wrong: Research firmly establishes a universal 90% debt/GDP danger threshold
distractors.why: the Reinhart-Rogoff 90% figure was an Excel error; sustainability is context-dependent

nodes.sample_question: State the countercyclical rule for fiscal policy across the business cycle, and what the Reinhart-Rogoff episode teaches about debt 'thresholds'.
nodes.failure_mode: Running procyclical policy (spending more in booms), or treating a debt threshold as a universal law.

nodes.subject: MACRO
nodes.concept: How banks create money (loans create deposits)
nodes.teaching_note: A myth-buster from the capstone: banks do NOT need deposits first to lend. When a bank makes a loan it creates TWO entries — a new deposit in the borrower's account and a matching loan asset — so the LOAN CREATES THE DEPOSIT. Banks are limited not by deposits but by CAPITAL and reserve/regulatory requirements (CRR, SLR, capital adequacy). Corollary: loan waivers are NOT free — the government compensates banks (taxpayer money) or banks absorb losses as provisions, weakening future lending (the NPA friction).

distractors.wrong: A bank must collect deposits before it can make a loan
distractors.why: the loan CREATES the deposit; banks are constrained by capital/regulation, not prior deposits

distractors.wrong: A government loan waiver is costless free money
distractors.why: someone pays — taxpayers compensate banks, or banks book losses as provisions (NPA friction)

nodes.sample_question: Explain 'loans create deposits' and why a farm-loan waiver is not actually free money.
nodes.failure_mode: Believing banks lend out pre-existing deposits (the simple multiplier story) — loans create deposits; capital/regulation bind.
